metric_rationale: This metric isolates 'conflict' trials where Tallying predicts Option A (because Option A wins on more features overall) but WADD predicts Option B (because Option B wins on fewer, but higher-validity features). We calculate the mean response on these specific trials. Tallying will produce a metric near 0 (choosing A), whereas WADD will produce a metric near 1 (choosing B), creating a maximal and highly reliable contrast between the two models.

This metric isolates the critical trials where the two theories make opposing predictions. In these trials, one option ('heavy') has only two positive features but they are the most valid ones (0.95 and 0.85), whereas the other option ('many') has three positive features but they are less valid (0.6, 0.55, 0.5). WADD tends to favor the 'heavy' option because the weighted sum of the two highly valid features is generally greater than the sum of the three less valid features. Tallying, on the other hand, ignores cardinal validities and strictly favors the 'many' option because 3 wins > 2 wins. The metric calculates the proportion of times the 'heavy' option is chosen on these critical trials. We expect a high value for WADD and a low value for Tallying.

This metric isolates 'conflict trials' where Tallying and WADD (assuming a baseline gamma=1) make strictly opposing predictions. For example, when one option wins on more total features (favored by Tallying) but the other option wins on the higher-validity features (favored by WADD). The metric calculates the proportion of choices on these conflict trials that align with the Tallying prediction. Under the Tallying theory, this proportion will be high (close to 1, minus noise); under WADD, it will be low (close to 0, plus noise).

Measures the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option with a positive rating on the most valid feature (feature 0), out of all trials where the two options differ on this feature. Tallying ignores feature validities and simply counts total wins, which in this specific experimental design leads it to choose against feature 0 on 5 out of 8 critical trials (yielding a baseline rate of 37.5%, pulled towards 50% by noise). WADD, on the other hand, weights feature 0 heavily due to its high validity, leading to a much higher rate of choosing the option that wins on feature 0 (approaching 100% for larger values of gamma).

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic. Since the features are presented in decreasing order of validity, TTB simply scans the features from first to last and chooses the option that wins on the first discriminating feature. The experimental design includes multiple 'compensatory' trials where the single best discriminating feature points to one option, but the sum of the remaining features points to the other. TTB will have a near-perfect match rate on these trials, whereas the Weighted Additive (WADD) model will frequently choose the opposite option due to its compensatory nature, resulting in a significantly lower TTB match rate.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chose the option with the higher total number of positive features (the 'Tallying' winner), specifically restricting the analysis to trials where this option is opposed by the Take-The-Best (TTB) heuristic (which always favors the option winning on the single most valid discriminating feature). Under TTB, this metric will be very close to 0, as subjects will almost never choose the Tallying winner when it conflicts with the most valid cue. Under the Weighted Additive (WADD) rule, this proportion will be substantially higher, because compensatory decision-makers will often allow multiple lower-validity cues to jointly outweigh a single higher-validity cue.

Through mathematical analysis of the parameter spaces, we find that for the vast majority of subjects (~95%), Probabilistic Take-The-Best (PTTB) will perfectly mimic the deterministic choices of Take-The-Best (TTB) because the exponential weighting function (gamma parameter up to 200) heavily polarizes the choice probabilities. Consequently, looking for trial-by-trial deviations fails because they only exist for a tiny fraction of low-gamma PTTB subjects, who end up inflating the variance without moving the mean sufficiently. 

The true, robust mathematical difference between the models lies in their uniform lapse rates: TTB's epsilon ranges up to 0.50 (expected adherence 87.5%), while PTTB's epsilon only ranges up to 0.25 (expected adherence 93.75%). By computing the subject's overall adherence to TTB and applying a hard threshold at 85%, we create a highly discriminatory binary metric. Approximately 40-50% of TTB subjects will fail to reach this 85% adherence threshold due to their higher lapse rates. In stark contrast, over 90% of PTTB subjects will comfortably clear it. This binarization perfectly exploits the difference in the noise parameter bounds, ensuring a massive mean difference between the theories while strictly bounding the between-subject variance.

Under the deterministic Take-The-Best (TTB) model, the probability of making a TTB-consistent choice is constant across all trial types (1 - epsilon/2). Thus, the difference in TTB match rates between trials where the TTB choice is supported by 3 features and trials where it is supported by only 1 feature should be exactly 0 on average. Under Probabilistic Take-The-Best (PTTB), features are sampled stochastically proportional to their exponential validities. When the TTB choice is supported by only 1 feature, the opposing coalition has 3 or 4 features, presenting a much larger combined probability mass to be sampled first compared to trials where the TTB choice is supported by 3 features. Therefore, PTTB predicts a significantly higher TTB match rate when 3 features favor the TTB choice than when only 1 feature does, yielding a strongly positive difference.
